payload.reason: The mechanics are accurate but the impact premise is wrong. The string-literal rail is deliberately scoped to the CLI flag surface, not a global invariant: the design note 2026-07-22-web-bind-address.md states 'Programmatic carrier consumers may select another hostname or address directly,' and the webserver docs/docs note 2026-07-28-api-browser-trust-boundary.md document 0.0.0.0 as 'deliberate network exposure' whose 'trusted-network assumption ... is now documented instead of implicit,' with 'reachability [being] the webserver binding's policy.' Reaching 0.0.0.0 through any alternate path requires the operator to author a cordis.patch.yml/--patch overlay (documented consequence, chosen by the operator) or an attacker to already have $CF_HOME write access (machine compromise), so it is not exploitable by a network or confused user. In the default shipped composition no --host flag means the row defaults to 127.0.0.1 and resolveLanTrust derives nothing, and the flag path is airtight (the schema z.union of z.const('127.0.0.1')/z.const('0.0.0.0') rejects every other spelling, so only the exact literal could even reach the rail). Finally, the 'auto-trusts every LAN IPv4' consequence is not a security regression but the fence's intended shape: the /api fence is explicitly a confused-deputy/DNS-rebinding defense, not an auth layer, so once the server is bound to 0.0.0.0 a LAN attacker reaches the socket directly regardless of fence entries; adding derived IP-literal entries narrows the rebinding gap rather than widening access. This is documented intended behavior, not a defect.

The mechanism is real and I confirmed it end to end: vite.config.ts:113 sets sourcemap:true, 25 .js.map files land in apps/web/dist with full sourcesContent, the emitted chunks carry live //# sourceMappingURL comments, and frontend-static's serveStatic serves any GET/HEAD file under distRoot with no extension allowlist while its MIME table deliberately maps '.map' -> 'application/json'. package.json files:["dist","!dist/**/*.map"] and .npmignore *.map only affect npm pack; check-workspace-constraints.ts:61-63 confirms maps are intentionally left on disk and merely kept out of the tarball. Nothing refutes the mechanism.

However the claimed IMPACT is overstated, so medium -> low. (1) The maps do NOT expose original first-party source: of 191 unique sources across all 25 maps, only two are genuine TypeScript (apps/web/src/main.ts, 421 chars of trivial bootstrap, and src/node-module-stub.ts, 481 chars). Every substantive first-party source is already-compiled packages/client/{ui-primitives,ui-slots,web}/lib/index.js -- and those packages publish lib/index.js publicly to npm verbatim (files:["lib/index.js",...], private:false), so the served map discloses no code the registry does not already give away. The real TSX mapping (tsdown.client.ts's client.js.map sourcemapPathTransform/browserSourcePath) is never in this dist, and publication-payload.ts forbids those maps from ever being packed. (2) No secret material: build defines inject only CF_CLIENT_* values (commit hash, title, profile), which are public and pinned by .cf-build/client-build-environment.json; a secret-pattern scan of all 25 maps found only React internals, HTML input types and shiki grammar keyword lists. (3) Default bind is loopback (cordis.patch.yml:125 host: !!js ctx.webStartup.host ?? '127.0.0.1'), so exposure is same-host by default, not LAN.

What actually survives is a hygiene/perf inconsistency plus a contradiction with the repo's own map-stripping policy -- multi-MB .map payloads fetched whenever DevTools is open on an origin the project otherwise keeps map-free. That is a real cleanup a maintainer would accept, but it is not the source-disclosure/secret-leak defect the finding frames, and it is not medium severity.

The deletion is unstaged (git status ` D vitest.e2e.config.ts`) so the file's last known content is still in HEAD and can be restored with `git show HEAD:vitest.e2e.config.ts` or `git checkout -- vitest.e2e.config.ts`. findings.title: exportConfig redaction flag is inverted: redactKeys=false writes a literal '***REDACTED***' placeholder as a real apiKey value
findings.detail: In BYOKEngine.exportConfig (lines 679-695), the spread `...(redactKeys ? {} : { apiKey: '***REDACTED***' })` has the branches exactly backwards relative to the flag's meaning. With redactKeys=true the apiKey field is dropped (correct redaction); with redactKeys=false — the documented way to get an unredacted export (e.g. a backup before moving machines) — no real key is ever emitted; instead the literal placeholder string '***REDACTED***' is placed in the apiKey field. Consequences: (1) an exported config file looks unredacted but contains only the placeholder, so an import round-trip registers '***REDACTED***' as a live key (addKey stores it verbatim, and it would be sent as the Authorization header to the provider), silently corrupting the config; (2) consumers wanting a true unredacted backup have no correct path via exportConfig and are pushed toward the unguarded getConfig(), which leaks plaintext keys (see the next finding). The codebase's own redaction seam (packages/settings/settings/src/redact.ts, used by host/apiproxy via settings.describe({ redactSecrets: true })) handles this correctly; byok.ts simply bypasses it. The correct code is `{ ...(redactKeys ? { apiKey: '***REDACTED***' } : { apiKey: originalApiKeyValue }) }` — but listKeys()/KeyInfo don't carry the raw key, so exportConfig currently can never reach it.

findings.title: getConfig() returns the live, unfrozen BYOKConfig containing plaintext API keys with no redaction
findings.detail: The public getConfig() method returns `this.config` typed as Readonly<BYOKConfig>, but Readonly is shallow and nothing is frozen at runtime. `keys` is `APIKeyConfig[]` with the raw `apiKey` field on each entry (packages/cf/src/types.ts lines 85-91), so any consumer can read every plaintext key and even mutate the underlying array/objects (the constructor keeps the caller's array reference via `config.keys ?? []`). Because exportConfig's unredacted path is broken by the inverted flag (***REDACTED*** always emitted), getConfig() is the only way to export real keys — callers doing config serialization, logging, or backup through it bypass every redaction mechanism the codebase otherwise enforces at wire boundaries ('Every wire surface MUST pass this' per SettingsDescribeOptions). This is unguarded secret exposure on a public API.

findings.title: Budget limits coerced with falsy || : a deliberate $0 daily/monthly budget silently becomes $100/$1000
findings.detail: In the constructor, `daily: this.config.budget.daily || 100` and `monthly: this.config.budget.monthly || 1000` treat 0 as 'unset'. A user or host configuring a hard-zero spend limit (or alertThreshold of 0) gets it silently replaced by the default 100/1000/80, so budget enforcement that should block all spend allows the full default budget. The checkBudgetAlerts() percentage math then reads against the wrong limit. Same falsy coercion pattern appears at construction for alertThreshold (`|| 80`). Unrelated to the redaction hint but a concrete correctness bug found in the same file.

payload.note: The hinted area was re-examined. The specific lost finding — a real secret landing in the exported config via exportConfig() — is NOT present: exportConfig() derives its keys from listKeys() (KeyInfo contains no apiKey field), so no plaintext key can leak through it, even with redactKeys=false (which emits the literal '***REDACTED***' placeholder instead). What IS present is the inverted branch logic in exportConfig() itself (reported as the high-severity finding), plus the unguarded secret exposure via getConfig() that the broken flag pushes callers toward. The sister seam packages are clean: packages/settings/settings/src/redact.ts implements structural secret removal correctly (removes role('secret') fields, enumerates paths, tested in packages/settings/settings/tests/redact.spec.ts), and packages/credentials/* is a reference-only seam whose types explicitly exclude secret values from configuration surfaces (CredentialInfo/CredentialRecordInfo 'never the value'). Note also that archive/cf-legacy/src/byok.ts contains an identical copy of the exportConfig defect, but was excluded per the task's path scope.

## 结论

该发现的机制描述属实，但作为缺陷特征描述有误。验证结果如下：

**机制正确的地方**：`packages/bundle/web-app/src/startup.ts:74` 的安全护栏只是一个简单的 `cmdstring` 比较，`packages/host/webserver/src/index.ts:75` 的 Layer Schema 确实接受 `0.0.0.0`，且 `packages/bundle/web-app/src/index.ts:132-139` 中的 `resolveLanTrust` 在绑定为 `0.0.0.0` 时，会将每个非内部 IPv4 地址自动添加到 `trustedHosts` 中。

**不成立的地方（影响分析）**：
1. 场景限定在 CLI 标志输入上是*故意为之* —— `.agents/notes/implemented/feature/2026-07-22-web-bind-address.md` 中记录了：“Programmatic carrier consumers may select another hostname or address directly”，并且 webserver 文档（`docs/subsystems/web-server.md`）将 `0.0.0.0` 定义为“deliberate network exposure（故意的网络暴露）”，且随之而来的是“没有 TLS、auth 或 origin policy（无加密、认证或源策略）”。
2. 设计笔记 `.agents/notes/implemented/architecture/2026-07-28-api-browser-trust-boundary.md` 指出：“reachability is the webserver binding's policy (`host: 127.0.0.1 | 0.0.0.0`)”，且“unauthenticated `0.0.0.0` deployment 的 trusted-network assumption 现在已被记录在案，而不是默许的”。LAN-IP 自动信任恰恰是这样设计的结构：绑定到全接口的组合会将获得的 LAN IP 字面量添加到 fence 中。
3. 围绕组合链的“绕过”需要操作员编写 `cordis.patch.yml`/`--patch` overlay（即，这是操作员有意为之的选择，其后果已记录在 webserver 配置文档中），或者需要攻击者已经获得 `$CF_HOME` 的写入权限（即，已经控制了机器）——对于网络攻击者来说，这不是一个可达的路径。
4. 在默认的 CLI 情况下，该行默认为 `127.0.0.1`（`cordis.patch.yml`：`host: !!js ctx.webStartup.host ?? '127.0.0.1'`），因此不会派生任何 LAN 信任；标志路径已完全封闭（Schema 会拒绝除了这两个字面量之外的任何其他宿主）。
5. “自动信任每个 LAN IPv4”也并非特权升级（privilege escalation）：一旦绑定到 `0.0.0.0`，LAN 攻击者无论如何都可以直接访问 socket —— fence 纯粹是浏览器混淆代理/DNS-rebinding 的防御手段，而不是认证层（与该发现的结论相反）。为部署使用的 IP 字面量派生 fence 条目反而*缩小*了 rebinding 防御缺口（根据设计笔记，IP-literal 的 Host 不能是 rebinding 的名称）。

综上：该护栏是已记录的、在 CLI 标志限定范围内故意应用的“深度建议” (deep advisory)，而全接口绑定选项则属于更有权威的配置层，且对其可预见的后果已有明确文档说明。任何维护者都会认为这是预期中的行为。

I've traced the whole chain end-to-end. Let me give the verdict.

**Mechanism — I confirmed every step the claim states:**

`apps/web/vite.config.ts:113` sets `sourcemap: true`, and line 119-120's own comment says rollup "writes each .map next to its js and references it by bare relative filename." The built `apps/web/dist` holds 25 `.map` files, and `assets/index-BKSebiLg.js` ends with a live `//# sourceMappingURL=index-BKSebiLg.js.map`.

`packages/host/frontend-static/src/index.ts` serves the whole dist root with **no** extension allowlist — `serveStatic` resolves the path, rejects only traversal, then `body = await readFile(target); type = MIME[extname(target)]`. The MIME table deliberately carries `'.map': 'application/json'`. So `/assets/index-*.js.map` returns 200, same-origin, content-type application/json. `packages/bundle/web-app/src/index.ts:233` mounts this against `require.resolve('@origin-ai/cf-web-frontend/dist/index.html')`, i.e. the checkout's built dist — the one that has the maps.

`package.json`'s `"files": ["dist","!dist/**/*.map"]` and `.npmignore` `*.map` only shape `npm pack`. `scripts/check-workspace-constraints.ts:61-63` spells out the split intent: "The Web build emits sourcemaps for browser debugging; publishing them is what the payload policy forbids, so the bundle ships without them." Nothing deletes them from the served directory, and `resolveDistIndex` points straight at it.

**But the impact is materially overstated.** I dumped every map's `sources`/`sourcesContent`: 191 unique sources, and the first-party ones are not "full original source." Only two entries are genuine TS — `apps/web/src/main.ts` (421 chars, a trivial mount-point bootstrap) and `src/node-module-stub.ts` (481 chars). Everything substantive that looks first-party is already-compiled `packages/client/{ui-primitives,ui-slots,web}/lib/index.js`, and those packages **publicly publish `lib/index.js` to npm anyway** (`files: ["lib/index.js","lib/invariant.js",...]`, `private: false`). The real TSX stays out: `tsdown.client.ts` emits `client.js.map` with true TSX mapping, but the vite dist consumes those as bundled *inputs*, and the payload policy forbids those maps from ever being published — the chain never reaches `.tsx`.

No secrets either. The build defines only inject `CF_CLIENT_*` values (commit hash, title, profile), which are all public and pinned by `.cf-build/client-build-environment.json`. A regex scan of all 25 maps for api_key/secret/password/token/PRIVATE KEY hits only React internals, HTML input types, and shiki grammar keyword lists.

And the host defaults to `host: !!js ctx.webStartup.host ?? '127.0.0.1'`, so by default this is same-host exposure, not LAN.

So: real mechanism, wrong impact story. What's left is a hygiene/perf wart — several MB of `.map` fetched whenever DevTools is open, on an origin the repo otherwise works to keep map-free — not a source-disclosure or secret-leak defect. A maintainer would likely fix it as cleanup, not as a security item.
